method: Convergence matrix, then narrative synthesis. Quantitative pooling was not offered because no finding estimates the same quantity on the same scale.

legend.D: dissonant (points the other way or changes with a definition)

conclusions.text: H1 cannot be tested as worded. No quote compares the AI with traditional voice automation by name, and no quote rates satisfaction. Q1 compares it with chat bots, Q3 refers only to having to "repeat yourself", and Q2 gives one indirect voice comparison: "sometimes when you are talking to a more of a robot, it sounds more like a robot voice".
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: Nine techniques agree and TC1-16 agrees in part, because it finds Q2 is one indirect voice comparison and that HE1-13, HE1-14 and HE1-15 overstate the gap when they say no quote compares at all. The repeat run of MM-10 disagreed on this target: Q7 on H1 was none in the original and oppose in the repeat, so the check for this conclusion is limited. The CK-17 spans that failed were labels, terms or one paraphrase, not source quotes, and the spot check found no mismatches. No person reviewed the results.

conclusions.text: Reactions to the AI are mixed among the six quoted participants. P1 (Q1), P2 (Q2) and P3 (Q3) speak well of it, and P4 (Q5) ends at "a really good process" after first wanting to speak to someone. P10 (Q4, Q8), P1 (Q6) and P5 (Q7) are unfavourable. The balance runs from a tie of three against three to four against one, depending on how P1 and P4 are coded and whether complaints tied to one context count.
conclusions.label: high
conclusions.reason: All ten techniques find favourable and unfavourable quotes. PE-02 finds four quotes with a positive cue and four with a negative cue under all six cleaning regimes, and TC1-17 finds that no change to the inclusion rules removes either side, although the balance moves. The repeat of MM-10 did not label general stance, so its Q7 difference on H1 does not test this conclusion. The checks passed, and no person reviewed the results.

conclusions.text: The reasons participants give for unfavourable reactions are several specific features, not one cause. They are the voice and accent (Q4, Q7), the length of the introduction (Q8), a stressful setting (Q7) and earlier experience with AI agents (Q6). Learning that it is an AI is not ruled out: P5 names "AI in its current state" in Q7 and P10 says "this sounds very much like an AI voice" in Q4. The link from Q7 to the motor claim scenario is inferred, not recorded.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: Most techniques name the same drivers. PE-02, HE1-15 and MM-10 only raise context as an alternative explanation and cannot test a cause, and TC1-17 notes that its combined rows cannot isolate one. TC1-16 finds that Q4 and Q6 do not fit a single context explanation, that Q7 names the AI, and that the scenario link is an inference, and this limits the label. These are stated reasons, not tested causes.

conclusions.text: H2 is untested on a strict reading, and no quote supports it. P10 says "I would've definitely have hung up at the intro." (Q8) and gives the length of the introduction as the reason. P5 would probably have hung up only after not getting a human (Q10). On a loose reading these two participants run against H2, but neither links the hang-up to learning that it is an AI, and the material does not say where the AI is disclosed. No quote says a participant would stay on the line. P4 in Q5 ends at a good process, which is about the process and not about hanging up.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: The techniques split. DM-02, HE1-13, HE1-15, TC1-16 and TC1-17 find H2 untested or the verdict dependent on definitions, while PE-02, CM1-05 and HE1-14 report it as contradicted and MM-10 and TC1-13 report it as mixed. TC1-17 shows the contradiction disappears if hypothetical statements are excluded or if the cause must be learning it is an AI. The repeat run of MM-10 disagreed on Q10 for H2 (original oppose, repeat neutral), so the check for this conclusion is limited.

conclusions.text: H3 is not supported, and two participants say they would ask for a human. P5 says "I would've asked for a human." (Q10) with no timing. P4 says "If I was gonna do it, that's probably where I would do it" (Q9), which is hedged and was said about the introduction in the material's note, not in P4's words, and Q5 says the wish to speak to someone fades as the process goes on. No quote says a participant would decline to ask. Under a strict reading of "immediately" the contradiction depends on one participant or on none.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: Eight techniques agree on the loose reading. TC1-16 and TC1-17 show it depends on two participants, on hypothetical and hedged statements, and on timing the quotes do not give, and TC1-17 leaves no contradiction when the strict rules are combined. This verification finding limits the label. The repeat of MM-10 agreed on all three H3 labels, and the other checks passed.

conclusions.text: The evidence has limits that every finding records. P8 and P9 have no quote, the basis for choosing the ten quotes is not given, every hang-up or human-request statement is a hypothetical reaction to a prerecorded scenario, and the material does not say where the AI is disclosed or which scenario each quote refers to apart from the motor claim reference in Q7. Each finding was produced by one coder. Counts describe the selected quotes, not how common a view is.
conclusions.label: high
conclusions.reason: All ten techniques state these limits, and the limits come from the material itself. The CK-17 spans that failed were labels, terms or one paraphrase, not source quotes, and the spot check found no mismatches, although its coverage is thin for HE1-14, HE1-15, MM-10 and TC1-13. No person reviewed the results.

answer.lead: The eight interviews do not support H1, H2 or H3 as worded. H1 cannot be tested because no quote compares the AI with traditional voice automation, and the reactions to the AI are mixed. For H2 and H3, no quote supports either hypothesis, and two participants say they would hang up or ask for a human, but those statements are hypothetical, partly hedged and not tied to learning that it is an AI or to a stated time. These are patterns within this sample only, and only six of the eight participants are quoted.
paragraphs: H1 (more satisfying than traditional voice automation): P1, P2 and P3 speak well of the AI, and P4 changes from wanting to speak to someone to calling it a good process. P10, P5 and P1 in a second remark are unfavourable, citing the voice, the accent, the length of the introduction and an imagined car accident. Depending on how P1 and P4 are coded, the balance is a tie or a lean of four against one. The favourable remarks compare the AI with chat bots, a robot voice and having to repeat yourself, and only the robot voice in Q2 is a voice comparison. The material therefore shows approval against poor earlier experiences and does not show the comparison H1 states. Confidence: high that the reactions are mixed, medium that H1 is untested, because the repeat run of MM-10 labelled Q7 on H1 differently from the original.

H2 (no immediate hang-up on learning it is an AI): P10 would have hung up at the introduction because it was too long, and P5 would probably have hung up only after being refused a human. Neither links the hang-up to learning that it is an AI. On a loose reading these two run against H2. On a strict reading no quote tests it, and no quote says anyone would stay on the line. Confidence: medium, because the techniques differ on this and the repeat run of MM-10 labelled Q10 on H2 as neutral where the original said oppose.

H3 (no immediate request for a human): P5 says they would have asked for a human, with no timing given. P4 says the introduction is where they would probably do it, hedges that statement twice, and says the wish passes as the process goes on. For a decision, the usable reading is that some participants want a route to a human early in the call, and the material cannot say how many of the eight would act this way. Under the strictest rules no contradiction remains. Confidence: medium.

The reasons participants give are less certain than what they say. They name the voice, the accent, the introduction, the setting and earlier experience, and P5 also names the AI itself. No technique tested a cause, and the link from the car accident remark to the motor claim scenario is inferred. Confidence: medium. All statements about hanging up or asking for a human are hypothetical reactions to prerecorded scenarios, P8 and P9 have no quote, the choice of quotes is not explained, and each finding used one coder. Confidence: high. The quote and pairing checks passed apart from six labels and terms placed in quotation marks, and the repeat runs differed on two stance labels. No person reviewed the results, which is not part of the plan at this decision-informing stakes and does not change the labels.
